newsitem.title: USA: Toys 'R' Us posts 57 percent profit jump.
newsitem.headline: Toys 'R' Us posts 57 percent profit jump.

text.p: Toys 'R' Us Inc. said Monday that a resurgent video game business and the re-release of the Star Wars movies trilogy helped its profits jump 57 percent in its fiscal first quarter.

The company, which calls itself the world's premier retailer of children's products, said its net income for the three months ended May 3 grew to $29.4 million, or 10 cents a share, from $18.7 million, or 7 cents a share.
It added that total sales increased 17 percent to $1.9 billion from $1.6 billion as sales in U.S. stores opened more than one year climbed by 8 percent.

The company, which operates more than 1,080 toy stores worldwide, including 680 in the United States, said its sales increases were driven by strong sales of video products as well as action figures and outdoor playsets.
It said it had very strong sales in Canada and Britain, both of which had double-digit same-store increases. It also posted sales gains in Japan, central Europe, France, Spain, and Australia.

"These sales increases were driven by the continued success of the video business, spurred by the introduction of Nintendo 64 in most of Europe, as well as innovative marketing and advertising programmes," it said in a statement.
The company added, however, that its Kids 'R' Us and Babies 'R' Us divisions experienced sales decreases in stores opened one year or more, primarily due to weak demand for children's apparel.
Sales were also hurt, as expected, during the transition of Baby Superstore locations into Babies 'R' Us stores, the company said.
It said the conversion of existing Baby Superstore locations to the Toys 'R' Us and Kids 'R' Us outlets was on schedule for completion next month.
The company currently has 212 Kids 'R' Us children's clothing stores and 82 Babies 'R' Us stores.
Toys 'R' Us stock was unchanged at $29.625 in heavy morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was among the most actively traded issues.
